YIELD-HUB dashboard export, end-of-season horizon, analysed November 2026

Where you forecast matters far more than which model you use

A statistical read of the sub-national crop yield benchmark: 14 deep-learning architectures and 5 models at 4 input resolutions, across 62 crop–country tasks.

Which model wins

Q1

Q1 Which architecture is best, overall and per crop?

patchtst and xlinear share the top. patchtst leads overall and clearly in wheat; maize is a near three-way tie between xlinear, tsmixer and patchtst.

Models joined by a grey bar are not significantly different. Seven of 14 are statistically tied with the best overall; timexer and the four other linear models trail furthest.

In resamples, patchtst is #1 in 65% of draws and xlinear in 31%; both stay in the top three in at least 97% of draws. The typical error of patchtst is 8% below the median model in the same task, dlinear’s 12% above.

Friedman test on NRMSE ranks across tasks: all χ²(13) = 269, p < 0.001, Kendall’s W = 0.33; maize χ² = 110, W = 0.24; wheat χ² = 179, W = 0.51. Nemenyi critical difference at α = 0.05: 2.52 (all), 3.35 (maize), 3.82 (wheat). Bootstrap: 2,000 resamples of tasks. P(#1) in maize: xlinear 34%, tsmixer 31%, patchtst 21%; in wheat: patchtst 87%.

Q2

Q2 Do transformers beat linear and CNN-LSTM models?

They beat the linear family by about 9% on average, but not CNN-LSTM. And family is not destiny: xlinear alone matches the best transformer.

The linear family’s weak average comes from dlinear, nlinear, olinear and rlinear. xlinear beats them by 17% and the median transformer by 6%.

The single CNN-LSTM performs like a typical transformer.

Paired Wilcoxon signed-rank tests on per-task log NRMSE ratios, Holm-corrected within each crop scope. Transformer vs linear family medians: −8.7% (95% CI −11.9 to −5.2%), matched-pairs rank-biserial r = −0.88, p < 0.001. Best transformer vs best linear: −0.6%, Holm p = 0.59. patchtst vs xlinear: −0.8%, Holm p = 0.93.

Q3

Q3 Is the winner the same for maize and wheat?

Mostly. The order is nearly identical, but maize is a flatter race, and patchtst and xlinear pull ahead mainly in wheat.

Within the 23 countries that grow both crops, patchtst and xlinear rank about 2.4 places better in wheat than in maize; nlinear ranks 2.7 places better in maize.

No single model’s shift survives multiple-testing correction; the interaction shows up only jointly.

Rank agreement between crops: Spearman ρ = 0.96, Kendall τ = 0.87 (p < 0.001). Model × crop interaction: permutation test swapping crop labels within the 23 shared countries, 20,000 permutations, p = 0.003. Per-model Wilcoxon on rank shifts, Holm: smallest p = 0.09 (nlinear).

Q4

Q4 Do the models beat simple baselines?

No. The best architectures only match climatology and the trend baselines, and every architecture loses to a 3-year rolling mean.

12 of 14 architectures are significantly worse than climatology; all 14 are significantly worse than the rolling-3 mean. patchtst wins 47% of tasks against climatology and 31% against rolling-3.

Even choosing the best model per task in hindsight beats the strongest baseline of that task in only 32% of tasks. The rolling-3 mean is the hardest baseline in 30 of 62 tasks.

Skill = 1 − RMSE(model) ÷ RMSE(baseline). Two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank tests of median skill = 0 per model and baseline, Holm-corrected across 56 tests; ▲ or ▼ marks p < 0.05. The hindsight row picks the best of 14 per task, so it is an optimistic upper bound.

Q5

Q5 How much is gained by picking the best model per country?

Little that can be realised. One model everywhere is within about 6% of the per-task winner, and tailoring the choice by crop or continent does not improve on that.

Twelve architectures win at least one task, but in a typical task only one other model comes within 5% of the winner. Picking the per-task winner needs hindsight.

A fixed bad choice is costly: always using dlinear adds a median 31%.

Selection strategies were evaluated leave-one-task-out: the model is chosen by mean rank on the other tasks (within the same crop, continent or both) and scored on the held-out task. Regret = NRMSE ÷ hindsight-best NRMSE − 1. Strategy vs one global model, paired Wilcoxon: per crop p = 0.11, per continent p = 0.63, per crop × continent p = 0.67.

Where models work

Q6

Q6 What explains performance most: country, crop or model?

The task. Country and crop explain 90% of the variation in log NRMSE; the choice of architecture explains 3.3%.

Skill against climatology already removes most of the country effect, and even there the task explains three times as much as the model (50% vs 16%).

The large model × country share for skill means rankings reshuffle from country to country.

Variance decomposition of the balanced 62 task × 14 model design. Task-level variance is split into country, crop and crop × country (averaged over entry order for the unbalanced crop–country part). Model main effect: F(13, 780) = 31.8, p < 0.001. Model × crop: F = 2.6, p = 0.002.

Q7

Q7 Are some continents systematically harder?

Yes for raw error, no for added value. African errors are about twice Europe’s, but the best model’s skill over climatology does not differ significantly between continents.

Higher NRMSE in Africa tracks lower, more variable yields that are hard for every method, baselines included.

xlinear ranks best in Africa and in the Americas, Asia and Oceania; patchtst ranks best in Europe. This difference in rankings is suggestive but not significant.

Kruskal–Wallis on task-level median-model NRMSE: H = 16.5, p < 0.001, ε² = 0.25; Dunn post-hoc (Holm) Africa vs Europe p < 0.001; within maize only p = 0.004. Best-model skill vs climatology: H = 3.0, p = 0.22. Model × continent ranking interaction, permutation test: p = 0.06 (maize only p = 0.43). The Americas, Asia and Oceania are pooled (11 tasks) because each has 1–4 tasks.

Q8

Q8 Does the admin level (NUTS-1, 2, 3) change accuracy?

No. The apparent trend is a continent effect: every NUTS-1 country is African and every NUTS-3 country is European.

Within Europe, NUTS-2 and NUTS-3 tasks do equally well; within Africa, NUTS-1 and NUTS-2 do too.

Across levels: Kruskal–Wallis p = 0.02, Jonckheere–Terpstra trend p = 0.04 (median NRMSE 0.44, 0.28, 0.25). Within Europe, NUTS-2 vs 3: Mann–Whitney p = 0.39; within Africa, NUTS-1 vs 2: p = 0.55. Best-model skill: Kruskal–Wallis p = 0.46. Admin level is defined for 50 of 62 tasks.

Why: data properties

Q9

Q9 Do more samples, years and regions improve accuracy?

Not on their own, because data-rich countries also have more varied yields. Once that is accounted for, 10× more training samples means about 11% lower NRMSE, and transformers gain the most.

Brazil, the US, Argentina and India have the most samples and the most heterogeneous yields, which hides the benefit of data.

With more data, tst and CNN-LSTM improve relative to their peers, while several linear models tend to fall behind. The transformer edge over linear models is about 4% in the data-poor half of tasks and 16% in the data-rich half.

Spearman correlations of task-level NRMSE and skill with log training samples, training years and log regions: all |ρ| ≤ 0.29, Holm p > 0.8. Adjusted OLS (HC3), log median NRMSE on log10 samples + training years + crop + continent + yield CV: β = −0.12, p = 0.02. Mixed model, log NRMSE with random task intercept: log samples × transformer −0.032 (p = 0.005), × CNN-LSTM −0.078 (p < 0.001), relative to linear. Per-model slopes, Holm: tst p = 0.02, cnnlstm p = 0.01.

Q10

Q10 Are models more useful where yields are low, volatile or weakly trended?

Skill over climatology does not depend on yield level, variability or trend. But where yields follow a trend or persist from year to year, a naive trend or rolling baseline beats every model.

In the third of countries with the weakest trend, the best model edges out all baselines (median skill +0.04); in the most strongly trended third it loses by 0.32.

The models seem to miss trend and persistence signals that simple baselines capture for free.

Task properties are back-calculated from the reported metrics: mean test yield = RMSE ÷ NRMSE, test variance = MSE ÷ (1 − R²), baseline RMSE = RMSE ÷ (1 − skill); all agree across models to within 0.03%. Spearman, best-model skill vs strongest baseline against trend strength: ρ = −0.63, p < 0.001. OLS with standardised predictors (HC3): trend strength β = −0.11, persistence β = −0.11, both p < 0.001, R² = 0.63. Part of this link is built in, because trend strength and the strongest baseline share the trend RMSE.

How: inputs and training

Q11

Q11 Does input resolution (daily to monthly) change accuracy?

Barely. Changes stay within about ±2%; monthly inputs are slightly worse, for every model alike.

The best resolution varies from task to task without a pattern, so it is not worth tuning per country.

Friedman test across resolutions within each model: patchtst p = 0.16, xlinear p = 0.66, tabpfn p = 0.42, tabdpt p = 0.06, tabicl p = 0.008 (W = 0.08; monthly 1.3% worse than dekad, Holm p = 0.04). Pooled over models on weekly, dekad and monthly: p = 0.01, W = 0.07. Model × resolution interaction, permutation test: p = 0.33. Bars: 95% bootstrap CI of the median.

Q12

Q12 Do untrained tabular foundation models match trained models?

Yes. tabpfn, with no training at all, is about 3–4% more accurate than trained patchtst and xlinear at the same input resolution. tabicl ties; tabdpt is 7–10% worse.

The tabpfn advantage comes mainly from wheat (−7.5%) rather than maize (−2.6%).

It is not limited to data-poor countries: the gap does not change with sample size.

Paired Wilcoxon on per-task log NRMSE, averaged over weekly, dekad and monthly, Holm across 6 pairs. tabpfn vs patchtst: −3.4% (95% CI −7.5 to −0.3%), p = 0.01, wins 61% of tasks. tabpfn vs xlinear: −4.1%, p = 0.03. Against the trained models’ daily runs: −3.2% and −2.1%, not significant after correction. Gap vs log samples: Spearman ρ = +0.08, p = 0.52.

Robustness

Q13

Q13 Do the conclusions hold across metrics and without the tiny countries?

The top tier holds; the #1 spot does not. patchtst, xlinear and tsmixer stay near the top in every variant, and the four weakest linear models stay in the bottom five.

Within a task, NRMSE, R² and all four skill scores are transformations of the same RMSE, so they rank models identically. Only SMAPE adds independent information, and it agrees.

Dropping small countries hands #1 to xlinear. Weighting by raw sample counts lets Brazil and the US dominate and lifts CNN-LSTM. Leaving out any single country never displaces patchtst.

Kendall’s W across the 7 metric rankings = 0.997; within-task Spearman between NRMSE and SMAPE ranks, median 0.97. Spearman between the main ranking and each variant: 0.90–1.00, except raw sample weighting at 0.78. Leave-one-country-out (39 runs): patchtst #1 in all; no model moves more than one place.

Methods and limits

  • Primary metric: NRMSE, ranked within each crop–country task. Six of the seven dashboard metrics rank models identically within a task (Q13), so NRMSE stands for them.
  • Each architecture has one result per task, with no seeds or folds. Between-model differences are judged against task-to-task variation only.
  • This data cannot test the dashboard’s headline question about process-based agronomic knowledge: there are no runs with and without it. Errors are only reported per country, so “region” means continent or admin level.
  • The Predictions tab holds demo data and is excluded. The Individual vs Pooled tab is empty.
  • “Hindsight best” selects on the test set and is an upper bound, not an achievable strategy.
  • Continent and admin level overlap heavily, so Africa-specific results rest on 11 maize tasks.
